course.title: Chemistry: Atoms to Reactions
course.description: Meet the particles, build a bond and keep every atom. Predict how much a reaction can make.
course.audience: An adult comfortable with arithmetic, fractions and simple ratios. Build a foundation in particles, bonding and chemical quantities.

paragraphs: Everything you can touch, from the water in a glass to the steel in a spoon, is built from a little over a hundred kinds of atom, joined in different numbers and arrangements. Chemistry is the study of those atoms, of the ways they hold together, and of what happens to them when one substance turns into another, as hydrogen and oxygen do when they burn to give water.

In a change of that kind the atoms are regrouped, but none is made and none is lost, and that fact makes chemistry a subject of careful counting. A formula records how many atoms of each element a substance contains, an equation records how the atoms are regrouped, and atomic masses together with the unit called the mole turn those counts into grams that can be weighed. With them you can work out, from the mass of one substance, how much of another it will react with, how much product can form and how much of a reactant will be left over.
outcomes: You'll be able to tell which element an atom is, and work out its neutrons, electrons and charge from a few counts.
You'll be able to write the formula of an ionic compound from the charges on its ions.
You'll be able to find the mass of a given amount of a substance, and the amount from a mass, using atomic masses and the mole.
You'll be able to balance a chemical equation so that every atom is accounted for.
You'll be able to say which reactant runs out first and how much product a reaction can make.

lessons.title: What makes an element?

steps.headline: An atom is a small, dense nucleus with lighter particles around it

lead.text: Almost all of an atom's mass is packed into a **nucleus** at its centre, which is tens of thousands of times narrower than the atom itself, and the rest of the atom is the region in which much lighter particles move around it.

This arrangement was worked out in 1911 by Ernest Rutherford, from experiments in which Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fired fast, positively charged particles at a thin sheet of gold foil. Nearly all of the particles passed straight through, so most of an atom's volume puts up almost no resistance, but a very few were turned back, and only a small, dense, positively charged centre could have done that.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows carbon and oxygen, each with its nucleus at the centre and rings of much lighter particles around it. The rings sort those particles into groups and are *not* paths that they follow. The labels at the right count three kinds of particle, which the next screen names, and the lines beneath the drawing summarise the counts.

steps.headline: Protons and neutrons make up the nucleus, and electrons surround it

lead.text: The three kinds of particle differ in electric charge. A **proton** carries a charge of +1, an **electron** carries a charge of −1, and a **neutron** carries none. Protons and neutrons together make up the nucleus, while the electrons stay around it because opposite charges attract.

Protons and neutrons have *almost* the same mass, and each is about 1,800 times as massive as an electron, so the mass of an atom is in effect the mass of its nucleus. The electron was identified in 1897 by J. J. Thomson, and the neutron not until 1932, by James Chadwick, because a particle with no charge leaves almost no trace in the instruments that detect the others.

afterFigure.text: In the figure, carbon has 6 protons and 6 neutrons in its nucleus, so the nucleus holds 6 + 6 = 12 particles, with 6 electrons outside it. Lithium has 3 protons and 4 neutrons, which makes 7 particles in the nucleus. **Only protons and neutrons** are counted as particles of the nucleus, because the electrons are not part of it.

steps.headline: The number of protons decides which element an atom is

lead.text: Atoms differ from one another in how many [[protons|Particles in the nucleus, each with a charge of +1. Met earlier in this lesson.]] they have, and **this count alone makes one element different from another**. The number of protons in the nucleus is the **atomic number**, and an **element** is a substance whose atoms all have the same atomic number. Every atom with 6 protons is carbon, every atom with 8 is oxygen and every atom with 3 is lithium, *however many* neutrons or electrons it happens to have.

That the proton count and nothing else sets the identity of an element was shown by Henry Moseley in 1913. He measured the X-rays given off by one element after another and found that their frequencies rose in regular steps, which he tied to a whole number for each element and identified with the positive charge of its nucleus. Arranging the elements by that number reproduces the order of the periodic table, including places where arranging them by mass gets the order wrong.

afterFigure.text: Each element also has a symbol of one or two letters, C for carbon, O for oxygen and Li for lithium, which appears at the centre of each drawing. The symbol names the element, and so it stays the same however the other two counts change.

steps.headline: Extra neutrons and missing electrons change the atom but not the element

lead.text: A lithium nucleus usually holds 3 protons and 4 neutrons. If it held 3 protons and 3 neutrons instead, it would be lighter, with 6 particles in place of 7, but its 3 protons would be untouched and the atom would still be lithium. A change in the neutron count therefore changes the mass of an atom and *nothing* about its identity.

Electrons can change as well. If a lithium atom loses one electron its [[nucleus|The small, dense centre of an atom, holding its protons and neutrons. Met earlier in this lesson.]] is exactly as before, so it is still lithium, but it now has 3 positive charges and only 2 negative ones, and so carries a net charge of +1. An atom or group of atoms with a net charge is called an **ion**, and forming one involves only the electrons and *never* the nucleus.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the three cases side by side, and the proton count is 3 in every one. The lines beneath the drawing change only where the neutrons or electrons change.

steps.headline: A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons

lead.text: An atom with no net charge is **neutral**, and it is neutral because each proton's +1 is cancelled by an electron's −1. The cancellation works only if the two counts are *equal*. A neutral chlorine atom has 17 protons, which carry a charge of +17 between them, and so it needs 17 electrons to carry −17 and bring the total to zero.

Give that atom one more electron and 17 protons face 18 electrons, so the charge is +17 − 18 = −1, which is the charge of a chloride ion. The neutrons play no part in any of these sums, since they carry no charge and are never counted when charges are added.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the neutral atom and the ion that results when it gains an electron. Both have 18 neutrons, and only the electron count and the charge differ.

steps.headline: Counting the electrons in a neutral lithium atom

workedSteps.text: Lithium has atomic number 3, so its nucleus holds 3 protons, and these contribute a total charge of +3.
A neutral atom has a total charge of zero, so its electrons must contribute −3 to cancel the nucleus.
Each electron carries −1, so it takes 3 electrons to make −3, and a neutral lithium atom has 3 electrons.

steps.headline: Counting the electrons in a neutral nitrogen atom

workedSteps.text: Nitrogen has atomic number 7, so its nucleus holds 7 protons, with a total charge of +7.
To bring the total charge to zero, the electrons must carry −7 between them, at −1 for each electron.

blocks.text: The grey trail that a pencil leaves on paper is graphite, a form of carbon, and a line half a millimetre wide is made of well over a million carbon atoms side by side. Each atom is far too small to see, yet its structure can be described by three counts, and one of them settles that the atom is carbon and nothing else.
Once you know which number settles what kind of atom you have, and which numbers change only its mass or its charge, you can read what an atom is made of from a few figures and say what it must be.

intro.whyItMatters: Every later idea in the course, from bonds to balanced equations, starts from knowing which particles an atom has.

recap.keyIdea: The number of protons, the atomic number, decides which element an atom is, while neutrons change its mass and electrons change its charge.

blocks.text: An atom has a nucleus of **protons and neutrons** with electrons around it, and its **atomic number** counts the protons alone. A neutron changes the mass and an electron changes the charge, but *neither* can change the element.

A [[neutral|An atom with equal numbers of protons and electrons, so no net charge. Met in “What makes an element?”.]] atom has as many electrons as protons, and an [[ion|An atom or group of atoms with a net charge, because its electrons and protons are unequal. Met in “What makes an element?”.]] differs from its atom only in its electrons, so **the nucleus of an ion is the nucleus of its element**.

recap.nextHook: Atoms of one element can still differ in their neutron count and so in their mass, and the next lesson shows how that difference is named and measured.

lessons.title: Same element, different mass

steps.headline: Atoms are weighed in atomic mass units

lead.text: An atom is far too light to be weighed in everyday units, since a carbon atom has a mass of only about 2 × 10⁻²⁶ kg. Chemists therefore use a unit of their own, the **atomic mass unit**, written u, which is defined as one twelfth of the mass of a carbon atom with 6 protons and 6 neutrons. That atom has a mass of exactly 12 u, by this definition.

A nucleus of 12 particles weighs 12 u, so each proton and each neutron has a mass *close to* 1 u, and measurement agrees: a proton is 1.007 u and a neutron 1.009 u, while an electron is only about 1/1,800 of 1 u. The mass of an atom in u is therefore **very nearly the number of particles in its nucleus**, because the electrons add almost nothing, and that count turns out to be the most useful way of labelling an atom.

steps.headline: The mass number counts the particles in the nucleus

lead.text: The number of protons and neutrons together is the **mass number** of an atom. Since the mass of an atom in u is very nearly this count, the mass number is the whole number nearest to the atom's mass. It is written after the name of the element, as in nitrogen-14, or as a small number above and to the left of the symbol, as in ¹⁴N.

Nitrogen has an [[atomic number|The number of protons in the nucleus, which names the element. Met in “What makes an element?”.]] of 7. The atom called nitrogen-14 has 7 protons and 7 neutrons, and the one called nitrogen-15 has 7 protons and 8 neutrons, so their mass numbers differ because their nuclei differ by one neutron.

afterFigure.text: **The mass number is protons plus neutrons**, and the atomic number is protons alone, so the mass number of an atom is *never* smaller than its atomic number. Neither of them depends on the electrons, which is why both stay the same when an atom becomes an ion.

steps.headline: Subtract the atomic number to find the neutrons

lead.text: The mass number is the total of protons and neutrons, so the neutron count is what remains when the protons are taken away: **neutrons = mass number − atomic number**. Uranium-238 has an atomic number of 92, so it has 238 − 92 = 146 neutrons, and its nucleus is one of the largest found in nature.

The mass number is a count, and so it is always a whole number, while the mass of the atom in u is only *close to* it: boron-11 has a [[mass number|The number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus. Met earlier in this lesson.]] of 11 but a mass of 11.009 u. The subtraction needs the mass number, which the name of the atom supplies, and the atomic number, which belongs to the element and which a table of elements supplies.

steps.headline: Finding the neutrons in magnesium-24

workedSteps.text: Magnesium-24 has a mass number of 24, so its nucleus holds 24 particles in all.
Magnesium has atomic number 12, so 12 of those particles are protons, and taking them from the total leaves the neutrons.
A magnesium-24 nucleus therefore holds 12 neutrons, as many as it holds protons.

steps.headline: Finding the neutrons in chlorine-35

workedSteps.text: Chlorine-35 has a mass number of 35, so its nucleus holds 35 particles in all.
Chlorine has atomic number 17, so 17 of those particles are protons, and the rest are neutrons.

steps.headline: Isotopes are atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons

lead.text: The [[atomic number|The number of protons in the nucleus, which names the element. Met in “What makes an element?”.]] fixes the element and only the neutron count is free to vary, so the atoms of a single element can have *different* mass numbers. Atoms with the same atomic number and different mass numbers are called **isotopes** of that element. Chlorine is a familiar case: chlorine-35 has 17 protons and 18 neutrons, and chlorine-37 has 17 protons and 20 neutrons.

The first evidence came in 1913, when J. J. Thomson passed a beam of neon ions through electric and magnetic fields and found that it divided into two paths, as though the gas held two kinds of atom with different masses. Frederick Soddy, who had been studying radioactive elements that no chemical process could separate, named such atoms isotopes that year, from Greek words meaning "the same place", because they occupy the same place in the periodic table.

afterFigure.text: Isotopes of one element share a chemical symbol, since the symbol names the element, and they differ in nothing but their neutron count and, with it, their mass number. In the figure the two chlorine nuclei have the same 17 protons.

steps.headline: An element's atomic mass is an average over its isotopes

lead.text: A sample of an element usually contains a mixture of [[isotopes|Atoms with the same atomic number and different mass numbers. Met earlier in this lesson.]], so the atomic mass quoted for the element is an *average* taken over its atoms. If two kinds of atom were equally common, the average would lie halfway between their masses, and a mixture of equal numbers of atoms of 35 u and 37 u would average 36 u.

In real chlorine the two isotopes are not equally common. About 75.8% of the atoms are chlorine-35 and 24.2% are chlorine-37, so the commoner isotope counts for more: 0.758 × 35 + 0.242 × 37 = 26.53 + 8.954 = 35.484, or about 35.5 u. This is called a **weighted average**, because each mass counts in proportion to its share of the atoms.

afterFigure.text: The average always lies **between the masses of the isotopes, nearer to the commoner one**. Boron, in the figure, has 19.9% boron-10 and 80.1% boron-11, which gives 1.99 + 8.811 = 10.801, or 10.8 u, and this is why a periodic table can list a mass that no single boron atom has.

blocks.text: Boron is listed in the periodic table with an atomic mass of 10.8 u, yet if you could weigh boron atoms one at a time, not one of them would come out at 10.8 u. Each would weigh very nearly 10 u or very nearly 11 u, and the figure in the table is the average of a mixture.

That mixture exists because the atoms of one element do not all have the same mass. The count that names the element leaves another count free to vary, so an atom needs a second label, and the mass of an element needs to be defined as a property of many atoms rather than of one.

recap.keyIdea: The mass number counts the protons and neutrons in a nucleus, isotopes of one element differ in their neutrons, and an element's atomic mass is the average over its isotopes.

blocks.text: The **mass number** is the number of protons and neutrons together, so **the neutron count is the mass number minus the atomic number**. Atoms of one element that differ in neutron count are [[isotopes|Atoms with the same atomic number and different mass numbers. Met in “Same element, different mass”.]]; they share a symbol and a chemical identity and differ only in mass.

A natural sample holds a mixture of isotopes, so an element's atomic mass is a *weighted average*, lying between the isotope masses and nearer the commoner one. Chlorine, which is 75.8% chlorine-35, averages about 35.5 u.

lessons.title: Gaining and losing electrons

steps.headline: The charge of an atom is its protons minus its electrons

lead.text: Every proton carries a charge of +1 and every electron a charge of −1, in a unit written *e*, so the charge of an atom or ion is found by adding up these contributions. The two kinds of charge cancel one for one, which leaves only the surplus, and so **the charge is the number of protons minus the number of electrons**. A [[neutral|An atom with equal numbers of protons and electrons, so no net charge. Met in “What makes an element?”.]] atom has equal numbers and a charge of zero, and neutrons never enter the sum because they carry no charge.

The sign tells you which kind of particle is in surplus: if protons outnumber electrons the charge is positive, and if electrons outnumber protons it is negative. The size of the charge is the size of the surplus.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows two examples. A beryllium atom has 4 protons, and with only 2 electrons left its charge is 4 − 2 = +2. A phosphorus atom has 15 protons, and with 18 electrons its charge is 15 − 18 = −3.

steps.headline: Losing electrons makes a positive ion and gaining them makes a negative one

lead.text: An atom can become an ion only by gaining or losing electrons, because a change in the protons would change the element. To find the electrons of an ion, start from the neutral atom, which has as many electrons as protons, and add or subtract. The beryllium atom in the figure began with 4 electrons and lost 2, leaving 2, while the phosphorus atom began with 15 and gained 3, giving 18.

An ion with a positive charge is a **cation**, and one with a negative charge is an **anion**, names that Michael Faraday introduced in 1834 along with *ion*. They record the way the ions travel in a solution when a current passes through it: cations drift towards the negative electrode, the cathode, and anions towards the positive electrode, the anode. A positive ion of a metal keeps the name of its element, as in sodium ion, while a negative ion of a non-metal takes the ending *-ide*, so that oxygen gives oxide, fluorine gives fluoride and chlorine gives chloride.

steps.headline: An ion keeps the nucleus of its atom

lead.text: Forming an ion moves electrons and **leaves the nucleus as it was**, so the protons, the neutrons and the atomic number of an ion are those of its atom. The ion belongs to the *same element*: a chloride ion has the 17 protons of chlorine, and its charge comes entirely from having 18 electrons around them.

The simplest case is hydrogen, whose atom has one proton and one electron. When the electron is lost, what remains is a bare proton with a charge of 1 − 0 = +1, and it is still hydrogen in the sense that matters, because its atomic number is 1.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the nucleus is the same in both drawings, and only the electron count and the charge below it change.

steps.headline: An ion's charge is written as a superscript, size first and then sign

lead.text: The charge goes after the symbol as a small superscript, with **its size first and its sign second**, as in Mg²⁺. A charge of one is written with the *sign alone*, so a sodium ion is Na⁺ and a chloride ion is Cl⁻. The superscript is the difference between the protons and the electrons, so with the element known it fixes the electron count: Na⁺ has 11 protons and one fewer electron, 10.

afterFigure.text: Pair each proton with an electron and the pairs cancel, and what is left over is the charge. In Na⁺ a single proton is left over, and in Cl⁻ a single electron is, which is why the first charge is +1 and the second −1.

steps.headline: Finding the charge of a magnesium ion

workedSteps.text: A magnesium atom has atomic number 12, so a neutral one has 12 protons and 12 electrons.
If the atom loses 2 electrons, 10 remain, and the 12 protons now outnumber them, which leaves a net positive charge.
The ion therefore has a charge of +2, which is written Mg²⁺, and it is still magnesium because its nucleus is unchanged.

steps.headline: Finding the charge of an oxide ion

workedSteps.text: Oxygen has atomic number 8, so every oxide ion has 8 protons.
An oxide ion has 10 electrons, so the electrons now outnumber the protons and the charge is negative.

blocks.text: Neither pure water nor a dry crystal of salt carries an electric current, yet a solution of salt in water carries it well. In the 1830s Michael Faraday, who was studying how current passes through solutions, concluded that such a solution must contain particles that move through it carrying electric charge, and in 1834 he named them ions, from a Greek word meaning "going".

An ion is an atom, or a group of atoms, that has gained or lost electrons, so that its positive and negative charges no longer cancel. Both the size of its charge and its sign can be read from two counts, the protons and the electrons, and once you can do that you can say what charge any ion carries and which ions are able to pair up in a solid such as salt.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to work out the signed charge of an ion from its protons and electrons.
intro.whyItMatters: The charge on an ion decides how it combines with others, which is the subject of the formulas in the lessons ahead.

recap.keyIdea: The charge of an ion is its number of protons minus its number of electrons, and forming an ion changes the electrons only.

blocks.text: The charge of an atom or ion is the number of protons **minus** the number of electrons, in units of *e*. A surplus of protons gives a positive charge, a [[cation|An ion with a positive charge. Met in “Gaining and losing electrons”.]], and a surplus of electrons gives a negative one, an [[anion|An ion with a negative charge. Met in “Gaining and losing electrons”.]].

Gaining or losing electrons is the only way an atom becomes an ion, so **the nucleus, and with it the element, is unchanged**: Mg²⁺ has the same 12 protons as a neutral magnesium atom and 2 fewer electrons.

recap.nextHook: The electrons that an atom gains or loses are not just any electrons, and the next lesson shows which ones, by looking at how an atom's electrons are arranged around its nucleus.

lessons.title: The outer electrons

steps.headline: Electrons occupy shells, and each shell holds a limited number

lead.text: The electrons of an atom are arranged in **shells**, which can be pictured as rings of increasing size around the nucleus. Each shell can hold only so many electrons: the first, nearest the nucleus, holds at most 2, the second holds at most 8, and for the first eighteen elements the third takes whatever remains, up to 8.

The electrons fill the shells in order, and the nearest shell is filled completely before any electron goes into the next. Nitrogen, with 7 electrons, therefore has 2 in the first shell and the other 5 in the second, an arrangement written 2, 5, while sodium, with 11, has 2, 8 and 1, written 2, 8, 1. The picture of shells goes back to Niels Bohr's atom of 1913, and it works as a counting rule: it does not show where an electron *really* is, but it gives the right number of outer electrons for these small atoms.

afterFigure.text: In the figure each ring is a shell and each dot an electron, so nitrogen has two rings and sodium three. Counting the dots on each ring gives the arrangement.

steps.headline: The outermost shell holds the valence electrons

lead.text: The electrons in the outermost occupied shell are the **valence electrons**, and they are the ones that matter in chemistry. They are the *farthest* from the nucleus and the most loosely held, so they are the electrons that an atom gives up, takes in or shares when it meets another atom, while the electrons of the inner shells stay with the nucleus. Sodium, arranged 2, 8, 1, has a single valence electron, which is the one that comes away easily, and ten inner electrons in filled shells that do not.

Phosphorus, with 15 electrons arranged 2, 8, 5, has 5 valence electrons, and sulfur, with 16 arranged 2, 8, 6, has 6. The number of valence electrons is **the number in the last occupied shell**, whatever the number in the shells inside it.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the outermost ring of each atom holds the valence electrons, and the rings inside it are full.

steps.headline: Arranging the electrons of silicon

workedSteps.text: A neutral silicon atom has 14 electrons, since its atomic number is 14.
The first shell takes 2 and the second takes 8, which together use up 10 of them, so 4 remain.
The 4 that remain go into the third shell, so silicon is arranged 2, 8, 4 and has 4 valence electrons.

steps.headline: Arranging the electrons of magnesium

workedSteps.text: Magnesium has atomic number 12, so a neutral atom has 12 electrons to place.
The first shell and the second are filled in turn, and whatever remains goes into the third.

steps.headline: Atoms with the same number of valence electrons behave alike

lead.text: Fluorine, with 9 electrons arranged 2, 7, and chlorine, with 17 arranged 2, 8, 7, have **the same number** of [[valence electrons|The electrons in the outermost occupied shell. Met earlier in this lesson.]], 7, although chlorine has an *extra* shell. The two behave alike: each tends to take in one electron, becoming F⁻ or Cl⁻, and each forms compounds of similar kinds.

This is the reason behind the columns of the periodic table. The elements in a column have the same number of valence electrons and so similar chemistry, and the table can be read as a list of the elements in the order in which their outer shells fill up and begin again.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the two atoms with an outer ring of 7 in each. Chlorine has one more ring inside it than fluorine, but it is the outer ring that each atom's chemistry depends on.

steps.headline: A full outer shell is a stable arrangement

lead.text: Neon, arranged 2, 8, and argon, arranged 2, 8, 8, have full outer shells, and they *hardly* react with anything. Argon was found only in 1894, by Lord Rayleigh and William Ramsay, and Ramsay named it from a Greek word meaning "idle" because it refused to combine with the other elements they tried.

Atoms of other elements react in ways that leave them with the arrangement of one of these gases. Sodium, arranged 2, 8, 1, reaches 2, 8 by losing its one valence electron, and becomes Na⁺ with 10 electrons. Chlorine, arranged 2, 8, 7, reaches 2, 8, 8 by gaining one electron, and becomes Cl⁻ with 18. Where an atom forms an ion, it is usually **the one that leaves a full outer shell**, which accounts for the charges met in the previous lesson.

blocks.text: A sodium atom has 11 electrons, yet in nearly all of its chemistry it gives up exactly one. Removing that one electron costs a certain amount of energy, and removing a second takes more than nine times as much, with a third needing more again, as though the first electron were held quite differently from the other ten.

It is held differently, because the electrons of an atom sit in layers at different distances from the nucleus, and sodium's eleventh electron is alone in a layer farther out than the rest. A simple counting rule tells you how many electrons sit in the outermost layer of any small atom, and that number tells you which ion the atom tends to form and which other elements it behaves like.

blocks.text: The first shell holds at most 2 electrons and the second at most 8, and for the first eighteen elements the third takes the remainder, so an atom's electrons are placed in order from the nearest shell outward. The electrons in the **last occupied shell** are its [[valence electrons|The electrons in the outermost occupied shell, the ones that take part in chemistry. Met in “The outer electrons”.]].
Atoms with the same number of valence electrons behave alike, and an atom tends to reach a *full* outer shell, as neon and argon already have. That is why sodium forms Na⁺ and chlorine forms Cl⁻.

lessons.title: Making a neutral formula

steps.headline: An ionic compound has no overall charge, so its ions come in a balancing ratio

lead.text: When a sodium atom gives an electron to a chlorine atom, the two become Na⁺ and Cl⁻, which attract each other, and the attraction between oppositely charged ions is called an **ionic bond**. A solid built from ions in this way is an **ionic compound**, and a crystal of it has no overall electric charge, since a lump of salt does not behave as though it were charged.

A crystal with no overall charge must contain positive and negative charge in *equal* amounts, so its ions come in a ratio that makes the charges add up to zero. In sodium chloride each Na⁺ carries +1 and each Cl⁻ carries −1, so one of each is enough: +1 + (−1) = 0. A single extra Cl⁻ would **leave the total at −1**, and the crystal would be charged.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows both cases. With one Na⁺ and one Cl⁻ the total charge is zero, and with a second Cl⁻ it is −1, so a ratio of one to two cannot be the ratio in sodium chloride.

steps.headline: The ratio of the ions is written as subscripts in the formula

lead.text: The ratio of one magnesium ion to two chloride ions is written MgCl₂. A formula of this kind lists the positive ion first and then the negative ion, and a small subscript after a symbol says how many of that ion there are in the ratio. A symbol with no subscript stands for **a single ion**, which is why Mg has none and Cl has a 2.

The numbers are always the *smallest* whole numbers that give the ratio. Sodium ions and chloride ions are in the ratio 1 to 1, so the formula is NaCl and never Na₂Cl₂, even though two of each would also balance, because the formula gives the ratio and says nothing about the size of any one crystal. The subscript belongs to the symbol before it, so in MgCl₂ the 2 refers to the chlorine alone.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the first case is magnesium chloride, with the three ions that its formula describes. The second is calcium oxide, in which both ions carry a charge of the same size, so that one of each balances.

steps.headline: When the charges differ, look for the smallest equal totals

lead.text: If the two ions carry charges of different sizes, one of each will *not* cancel. A lithium ion carries +1 and an oxide ion −2, so a single oxide ion needs two lithium ions beside it to bring the total to zero, and the compound has the ratio 2 to 1 and the formula Li₂O.

When neither charge divides evenly into the other, look for the smallest total that both divide into. Aluminium forms Al³⁺ and sulfur forms S²⁻, and the smallest number that 3 and 2 both divide into is 6, which takes two Al³⁺ to make +6 and three S²⁻ to make −6. The ratio is then 2 to 3 and the formula is Al₂S₃. Each ion's charge, with its sign ignored, **becomes the subscript of the other ion**, and this follows from the balance itself, since the positive total (number of cations times their charge) must equal the negative total. The swap can leave a common factor, as it does for Ca²⁺ and O²⁻, which would give Ca₂O₂, and the numbers must then be reduced to the smallest whole numbers, CaO.

steps.headline: Finding the formula of sodium sulfide

workedSteps.text: Sodium forms Na⁺, with a charge of +1, and sulfur forms S²⁻, with a charge of −2.
One sulfide ion carries −2, and one sodium ion cancels only +1 of that, so it takes two sodium ions for each sulfide ion.
The simplest ratio is 2 sodium ions to 1 sulfide ion, which is written Na₂S, with the 1 for sulfur left unwritten.

steps.headline: Finding the formula of aluminium oxide

workedSteps.text: Aluminium forms Al³⁺ and oxygen forms O²⁻, and the smallest total charge that both +3 and −2 divide into is 6.
Three O²⁻ ions carry −6 between them, and the aluminium ions must supply +6 to balance them.

steps.headline: A formula unit is the smallest group of ions with the right ratio

lead.text: An ionic crystal is a repeating pattern of ions with no beginning or end, so it contains no separate molecules, and the formula of an [[ionic compound|A solid built from oppositely charged ions. Met earlier in this lesson.]] does not describe one. It describes the smallest group of ions that has the correct ratio, which is called a **formula unit**. One formula unit of NaCl is one Na⁺ and one Cl⁻, and one formula unit of MgCl₂ is one Mg²⁺ and two Cl⁻, which makes three ions altogether.

The formula unit is a way of *counting*. In the crystal the ions alternate, and each Na⁺ is touched by six Cl⁻, none of which belongs to it any more than the others do. To count the ions in a formula unit, add the subscripts, reading a missing subscript as 1.

blocks.text: Table salt is written NaCl, which looks like a molecule made of one sodium atom joined to one chlorine atom. When William Lawrence Bragg and his father William Henry Bragg used X-rays to find how the particles are arranged in a salt crystal, in 1913, they found no such pairs. Each sodium ion has six chloride ions as its nearest neighbours and each chloride ion has six sodium ions, and the crystal is a pattern of ions that repeats in every direction.

The formula therefore says something more modest than it seems to: it gives the ratio of the ions in the crystal, one sodium ion for every chloride ion. That ratio is not arbitrary, because it is the one that makes the whole crystal electrically neutral, and it can be found for any pair of ions from their charges.

intro.whyItMatters: Writing a formula correctly is the first step in every calculation with a compound, from counting atoms to finding its mass.

recap.keyIdea: An ionic compound has no overall charge, so its ions are in the smallest whole-number ratio that makes the positive and negative charges equal.

blocks.text: A crystal of an ionic compound is neutral, so its positive and negative charges must be equal, and **the formula gives the smallest whole-number ratio of ions that achieves it**. When the charges differ, find the smallest total that both divide into: two Al³⁺ and three S²⁻ both give 6, and the formula is Al₂S₃.

The formula describes a [[formula unit|The smallest group of ions with the correct ratio, such as one Na⁺ and one Cl⁻ for NaCl. Met in “Making a neutral formula”.]], not a molecule, because the crystal is a continuous pattern of ions, and the number of ions in a unit is the sum of the subscripts.

lessons.title: Sharing electron pairs

steps.headline: Atoms can share a pair of electrons instead of handing them over

lead.text: A hydrogen atom has one electron, and the first [[shell|One of the rings of electrons around a nucleus; the first holds at most 2. Met in “The outer electrons”.]] holds two, so the atom is a single electron short of a full shell. Hydrogen has no electron to spare, so it cannot reach a full shell by giving its electron to another atom, yet two hydrogen atoms still join to make the molecule H₂. They do so by putting one electron each into a pair that **both atoms share**, and each atom then counts the whole pair among the electrons around it, which gives each a full first shell.

A shared pair of electrons that holds two atoms together is a **covalent bond**, and a group of atoms joined by covalent bonds is a **molecule**. The name *covalent* was given by Irving Langmuir in 1919. Where an ionic compound is held together by ions that have taken or lost electrons, a molecule is held together by atoms that keep their electrons and share some of them, which is how most pairs of non-metal atoms combine.

steps.headline: A Lewis drawing shows a shared pair as a line and an unshared pair as two dots

lead.text: The simplest way to show who shares what is a **Lewis drawing**, named for Gilbert N. Lewis, who proposed in 1916 that a chemical bond is a pair of electrons held in common by two atoms. Each atom is written as its symbol, a shared pair is drawn as a line between the two symbols, and a pair of [[valence electrons|The electrons in the outermost occupied shell. Met in “The outer electrons”.]] that is *not* shared is drawn as two dots beside its own atom, where it is called a **lone pair**.

In the chlorine molecule, Cl–Cl, each atom has 7 valence electrons, which makes 14 in all. Two of them form the shared pair, and the other 12 form six lone pairs, three on each atom. Each atom therefore has three lone pairs and one shared pair around it, and so 8 electrons, a full outer shell.

steps.headline: Atoms can share two or three pairs

lead.text: Some atoms need more than one electron to complete their shells, and they can share more than one pair. Two atoms joined by one shared pair have a **single bond**, drawn as one line, those joined by two shared pairs have a **double bond**, drawn as two lines, and those joined by three have a **triple bond**, drawn as three. Every line is one shared pair, so the number of lines between two atoms is the number of pairs they share.

Since each pair holds two electrons, **the number of shared electrons is twice the number of lines**. Atoms in a molecule can share electrons in this way with several neighbours at once, and an atom counts *every* pair it shares toward its own shell, whichever neighbour it is shared with.

steps.headline: Counting the shared electrons in oxygen

workedSteps.text: Oxygen gas is made of O₂ molecules, in which the two atoms are joined by a double bond.
A double bond is two shared pairs, and each pair holds two electrons.

steps.headline: Electrons that are not shared still belong to the count

lead.text: The electrons that an atom keeps to itself, in lone pairs, are called **nonbonding electrons**, and they are counted in the same way: two for *every* lone pair. A molecule's valence electrons are all accounted for by its shared pairs and its lone pairs, so the shared electrons and the nonbonding electrons together equal the total.

Oxygen shows the two kinds together. Each oxygen atom has 6 valence electrons, which makes 12 in the molecule. Four of these are shared in the double bond, and the other 8 are the nonbonding electrons, which sit in four lone pairs, two on each atom. Each atom has 4 nonbonding and 4 shared electrons around it, so 8 in all.

afterFigure.text: The figure gives the counts for hydrogen, which has no lone pairs, and oxygen, which has two on each atom.

lessons.orientation: How atoms share electron pairs, and how to count shared and nonbonding electrons in a Lewis drawing.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Hydrogen gas is made of particles that each contain two atoms, H₂, and yet no electron has passed from one atom to the other. Each atom has only one electron, and neither would gain a full shell by giving it up, so the ionic picture of the last lesson cannot explain what holds the pair together.

In 1916 Gilbert N. Lewis proposed that the two atoms are bound by a pair of electrons that belongs to both, so that each atom can count the pair as part of its own shell. The idea explains how atoms with the same appetite for electrons can still bond, and it gives a way of counting the electrons around each atom that you can do with a pencil.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a Lewis drawing and count a molecule's shared and nonbonding electrons.
intro.whyItMatters: Reading bonds correctly shows what a molecule is made of, which the next lesson needs in order to count the atoms in a formula.

recap.keyIdea: A covalent bond is a pair of electrons shared by two atoms, shown as a line, and a pair that belongs to one atom alone is a lone pair.

blocks.text: A **covalent bond** is a shared pair of electrons, and a Lewis drawing shows each one as a line, with a [[lone pair|A pair of valence electrons that belongs to one atom and is not shared, drawn as two dots. Met in “Sharing electron pairs”.]] drawn as two dots. A double bond is two shared pairs and a triple bond is three, so **the shared electrons are twice the number of lines**.
The electrons around an atom are its shared pairs, which it counts in full, together with its lone pairs, and for small atoms the total is a full shell: 8 for chlorine and oxygen, and 2 for hydrogen.

recap.nextHook: A molecule's formula says how many atoms of each element it contains, and the next lesson shows how to count the atoms in a formula, with the numbers written in front of it.

lessons.title: Reading a chemical formula

steps.headline: A formula counts the atoms in one molecule or formula unit

lead.text: A chemical formula writes each element by its symbol, a convention that goes back to Jöns Jacob Berzelius, who proposed in 1813 that each element be written with the first letter or two of its name in Latin, so that iron, *ferrum*, became Fe. A small number written after a symbol, lowered beside it, is a **subscript**, and it gives the number of atoms of that element in one [[molecule|A group of atoms joined by covalent bonds. Met in “Sharing electron pairs”.]]. A symbol with no number after it stands for a single atom.

Carbon dioxide, CO₂, has one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms, which makes three atoms in all, and the total for any formula is found by adding the counts for its elements. The formula of an ionic compound is read in the same way, and what it counts is one [[formula unit|The smallest group of ions with the correct ratio. Met in “Making a neutral formula”.]]: CaCl₂ is one calcium and two chlorine, three in all.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows one unit of each substance, with the count of each kind of atom beneath the drawing.

steps.headline: A number in front of a formula multiplies every atom in it

lead.text: A number written in front of a formula is a **coefficient**, and it says how many molecules or formula units there are. The line 2 CO₂ describes two molecules of carbon dioxide, so every count in the formula is *doubled*: 2 × 1 = 2 carbon atoms and 2 × 2 = 4 oxygen atoms, six atoms in all. With no coefficient written, there is one.

The total number of atoms of an element is therefore the coefficient times the subscript: **the coefficient multiplies everything in the formula that follows it**. The two numbers do different jobs, the subscript counting the atoms inside one unit and the coefficient counting the units, which is why a count needs both.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows sodium oxide, Na₂O, at two different amounts. Moving the slider changes the number of units, and the counts beneath the drawing change in step.

steps.headline: Counting the atoms in 3 H₂SO₄

workedSteps.text: One molecule of H₂SO₄ has 2 hydrogen atoms, 1 sulfur atom and 4 oxygen atoms, which is 7 atoms in all.
The coefficient 3 means three such molecules, so each count is multiplied by 3.
Altogether there are 6 + 3 + 12 = 21 atoms, which is the same as 3 × 7.

steps.headline: Counting the oxygen atoms in 2 Al₂O₃

workedSteps.text: One formula unit of Al₂O₃ has 2 aluminium atoms and 3 oxygen atoms.
The coefficient 2 means two formula units, so the oxygen count is multiplied by 2.

steps.headline: A subscript names the substance and a coefficient counts how much of it there is

lead.text: A subscript is part of the identity of a substance, so changing it gives a different substance. H₂O is water, while H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, a liquid used as a bleach and a disinfectant, and CO₂ is the gas we breathe out, while CO is carbon monoxide, which is poisonous. In each pair the atoms are the same and the molecules are *not*.

A [[coefficient|A number in front of a formula giving how many molecules or formula units there are. Met earlier in this lesson.]] changes *only* the amount. Two molecules of water are 2 H₂O, and they are still water. A subscript **names the substance**, and a coefficient **counts how much of it there is**, so when a count of atoms has to change, as it will in the lessons on equations, the coefficient is the number to change, and the subscripts stay as they are.

blocks.text: Water is written H₂O and sulfuric acid H₂SO₄, and a chemist reads such a string as a count of atoms, element by element. Put a number in front, as in 4 H₂O, and the line describes four molecules at once, with eight hydrogen atoms and four oxygen atoms between them.

The small number inside a formula and the large number before it do different jobs, and mixing them up changes what substance is meant and not only how much there is. Kept apart, the two numbers tell you how many atoms of each element any line of chemical writing stands for.

intro.whyItMatters: Counting atoms from a formula is how every equation is checked, so the next lessons use it again and again.

recap.keyIdea: A subscript counts the atoms of an element in one unit of a substance, and a coefficient counts the units, so the total is their product.

blocks.text: A [[subscript|A small number after a symbol giving the atoms of that element in one unit of the substance. Met in “Reading a chemical formula”.]] counts the atoms of an element in **one** molecule or formula unit, and a [[coefficient|A number in front of a formula giving how many molecules or formula units there are. Met in “Reading a chemical formula”.]] says how many units there are. The atoms of an element in a whole line are the coefficient times the subscript, added up over every element for a total.
A subscript **names the substance** and a coefficient **counts how much of it there is**, which is why only the coefficient can be changed when an equation has to be balanced.

lessons.title: Adding atomic masses

steps.headline: Each element has an atomic mass, and that is the number to add

lead.text: The mass of an atom is given in the atomic mass unit, and the mass listed for an element is **an average** over its [[isotopes|Atoms of one element with different mass numbers. Met in “Same element, different mass”.]], which is why the number is not always whole: carbon is listed as 12.011 u, oxygen as 15.999 u and chlorine as 35.45 u. The idea of tabulating relative masses goes back to John Dalton, who drew up the first such table in 1803, taking hydrogen as 1.

Whole-number masses are close enough for most of what follows, so problems in this course use rounded values, always *stated in the problem itself*. Chlorine is the one exception, kept at 35.5 u, because the average of its isotopes lies almost exactly halfway between 35 and 36, and rounding it to a whole number would introduce a larger error than for any other element in the table.

steps.headline: The mass of a formula is the sum of the masses of its atoms

lead.text: A molecule or formula unit has the mass of the atoms that make it up, so its mass is found by adding their atomic masses, one for *every* atom the formula contains. The result is the **formula mass**, in u. Oxygen gas, O₂, has two oxygen atoms of 16 u each, so its formula mass is 2 × 16 = 32 u, and hydrogen chloride, HCl, has one hydrogen atom and one chlorine atom, so its formula mass is 1 + 35.5 = 36.5 u.

The subscripts decide how many times each mass is added: every atom in the formula contributes its own mass, so **a subscript of 2 means that the atomic mass is added twice**. For sodium oxide, Na₂O, that is 23 + 23 + 16 = 62 u. The calculation is the same for a molecule and for an ionic compound, where the formula mass is the mass of one formula unit.

steps.headline: Finding the formula mass of SO₂

workedSteps.text: Sulfur dioxide, SO₂, contains 1 sulfur atom and 2 oxygen atoms. The atomic masses are S = 32 u and O = 16 u.
Each oxygen atom contributes 16 u and there are two of them, so the oxygen contributes 2 × 16 u.
Adding the one sulfur atom's 32 u to the oxygen's 32 u gives the formula mass.

steps.headline: Finding the formula mass of CO₂

workedSteps.text: Carbon dioxide, CO₂, contains 1 carbon atom and 2 oxygen atoms. The atomic masses are C = 12 u and O = 16 u.
Each atom contributes its own mass, so the formula mass is 1 × 12 plus 2 × 16.

steps.headline: With several elements, work through the formula one element at a time

lead.text: The [[formula mass|The sum of the atomic masses of every atom in a formula, in u. Met earlier in this lesson.]] of a longer formula is easier to find if you take it *one element at a time*, and for each element multiply the number of its atoms by the mass of one atom. A small table keeps the working in order, with a row for each element and the subtotals added at the end.

Ethanol, C₂H₆O, has 2 carbon atoms, 6 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom, which give 24 u, 6 u and 16 u, and a total of 46 u. Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, has larger counts but the same layout, and its total is 72 + 12 + 96 = 180 u. **The only things that change** from one formula to the next are the elements and their counts, and each row still reads atoms times mass.

steps.headline: Use the atomic masses that the problem states

lead.text: Tables of atomic masses differ in how far they round, and the answers differ a little with them. Water comes to 2 × 1 + 16 = 18 u with the rounded masses used here, and to 2 × 1.008 + 15.999 = 18.015 u with more figures. Neither is wrong, but they are *different* approximations, and a problem that lists its masses is asking for the answer those values give.

For this reason **use the atomic masses stated in the problem, and not the ones you remember**. If none are stated, the rounded values in the table of this lesson are the ones to use. The habit also avoids a mismatch that is easy to miss: a chlorine mass of 35.5 u in one line and 35 u in the next would give two different answers to the same question.

lessons.orientation: How to add atomic masses, with the right counts, to get the mass of a molecule or formula unit.

blocks.text: A molecule of oxygen has a mass of about 5.3 × 10⁻²⁶ kg, which is not a number anyone wants to carry through a calculation. In atomic mass units the same molecule is simply 32 u, twice the 16 u of a single oxygen atom, because a molecule has, to a very close approximation, the mass of the atoms it contains.

A formula already says how many atoms of each element a molecule has, so once each kind of atom has a mass, the mass of the whole molecule comes from multiplying each atomic mass by its count and adding the results. With that sum you can compare the masses of different substances molecule for molecule, and it is the number that later turns a count of molecules into a mass in grams.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the formula mass of any substance from its formula and a list of atomic masses.
intro.whyItMatters: Formula mass is the bridge between counting atoms and weighing a chemical, which the next lesson crosses.

recap.keyIdea: The formula mass is the sum of the atomic masses of every atom in the formula, with each mass added once for each atom.

blocks.text: The **formula mass** is the sum of the atomic masses of all the atoms in a formula, and **each mass is added as many times as its subscript says**: CO₂ is 12 + 2 × 16 = 44 u. For a formula with several elements, a row for each element, atoms times mass, keeps the working in order.

Atomic masses are [[averages over isotopes|Each element's atomic mass is the average of its isotopes, weighted by how common they are. Met in “Same element, different mass”.]], and tables round them differently, so the masses a problem states are the ones to use.

recap.nextHook: The mass of one molecule is far too small to weigh, so the next lesson introduces a unit that counts molecules in numbers large enough that the formula mass becomes a mass in grams.

lessons.title: From moles to mass

steps.headline: A mole is a fixed, very large number of particles

lead.text: Atoms are so small that any amount of matter you can weigh holds an enormous number of them, so chemists count in a unit of their own, the **mole**, written mol. One mole is exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ particles, a number called the **Avogadro constant**, and it plays the part that 12 plays in a dozen: it is simply *how many* make one unit. Twelve grams of carbon-12 hold very nearly one mole of atoms.

The particles may be atoms, molecules or ions, and the name of the substance says which. A mole of carbon is that many carbon atoms, and a mole of sodium chloride is that many [[formula units|The smallest group of ions with the correct ratio. Met in “Making a neutral formula”.]]. The constant is named for Amedeo Avogadro, who proposed in 1811 that equal volumes of different gases under the same conditions hold equal numbers of molecules, although its value was pinned down only in the early 1900s, by experiments such as those of Jean Perrin, who proposed the name.

steps.headline: The mass of one mole, in grams, is the formula mass

lead.text: The mole is defined so that the mass of one mole of a substance, in grams, has the same number as its [[formula mass|The sum of the atomic masses of every atom in a formula, in u. Met in “Adding atomic masses”.]] in u. Magnesium atoms have a mass of 24 u, and one mole of magnesium has a mass of 24 g, while sodium chloride has a formula mass of 58.5 u and one mole of it has a mass of 58.5 g. The mass of one mole is the **molar mass**, written M, and its unit is grams per mole, g/mol.

The numbers match because of the size of the unit: one u is *very nearly* 1/(6.02214076 × 10²³) of a gram, so a mole of particles that each weigh 24 u weighs 24 g. That is what makes the mole useful, since the formula mass found in the previous lesson becomes a mass that can be weighed out on a balance, and **the mass of any amount is the amount times the molar mass**.

afterFigure.text: In the figure, one mole of magnesium has a mass of 24 g and three moles have a mass of 3 × 24 = 72 g. The molar mass stays the same, and only the amount changes.

steps.headline: Finding the mass of 3 mol of sodium chloride

workedSteps.text: The molar mass of NaCl is the sum of the atomic masses of sodium and chlorine, which gives the mass of one mole in grams.
Three moles is three times as much, so the amount is multiplied by the molar mass.
The unit mol cancels and leaves grams, so the mass is 175.5 g.

steps.headline: Finding the mass of 2 mol of nitrogen gas

workedSteps.text: Nitrogen gas is N₂, with two atoms of 14 u each, so its molar mass is 2 × 14 g/mol.
Two moles is twice the mass of one mole.

steps.headline: To find the moles from a mass, divide by the molar mass

lead.text: The relation can be turned round: **the amount in moles is the mass divided by the molar mass**. Magnesium oxide, MgO, has a [[molar mass|The mass of one mole of a substance, in grams per mole. Met earlier in this lesson.]] of 24 + 16 = 40 g/mol, so 100 g of it is 100 ÷ 40 = 2.5 mol. The units guide the calculation, because grams divided by grams per mole leaves moles, whereas grams multiplied by grams per mole would leave a unit that means nothing.

Together the two relations connect a mass that can be weighed with an amount that can be counted in a reaction, and every calculation in the remaining lessons passes through that step. A quick check is to ask whether the answer is sensible: a mass larger than the molar mass has to be *more than* one mole.

afterFigure.text: In the figure, 40 g of magnesium oxide is exactly one mole and 100 g is two and a half.

steps.headline: A mole of molecules contains moles of atoms

lead.text: The subscripts of a formula count atoms, and since a mole of molecules is the same number of molecules whatever they are, the subscripts also count *moles of atoms*. One mole of MgCl₂ contains 1 mol of magnesium and 2 mol of chlorine, and 2 mol of MgCl₂ contains 2 mol of magnesium and 4 mol of chlorine.

The reasoning is that each of the 6.02214076 × 10²³ formula units in a mole has 2 chlorine atoms, so there are twice as many chlorine atoms as formula units, and the doubling carries over from atoms to moles. A formula therefore **links the amount of a compound to the amount of each element in it**, which the later lessons use when an equation is read as a ratio of moles.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows one mole and two moles of magnesium chloride. The molar mass is 95 g/mol, so the masses are 95 g and 190 g.

lessons.orientation: What a mole counts, how molar mass links moles to grams, and how formulas count moles of atoms.

blocks.text: A carbon atom has a mass of about 2 × 10⁻²³ g, so a piece of carbon that a balance can weigh, say 12 g, holds about 6 × 10²³ atoms. A count of that size is not one that anyone can make by counting, and it is far too large to write out atom by atom in a calculation.

A number of that size calls for a unit of its own, and the unit is chosen so that the mass in grams of that many particles is the formula mass already found in the last lesson. The choice turns a count of particles into a mass that can be weighed on a balance, and a weighed mass back into a count.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to convert between an amount in moles and a mass in grams, and count moles of atoms.
intro.whyItMatters: Every reaction is measured in grams and understood in moles, so converting between the two is the step the rest of the course relies on.

recap.keyIdea: A mole is 6.02214076 × 10²³ particles, its mass in grams is the formula mass, and so mass is amount times molar mass.

blocks.text: A **mole** is a fixed number of particles, and the mass of one mole in grams is the [[formula mass|The sum of the atomic masses of every atom in a formula, in u. Met in “Adding atomic masses”.]], called the molar mass. So **mass = moles × molar mass**, and moles = mass ÷ molar mass, with the units doing the checking.

Because a mole of molecules has the same number of molecules whatever the substance, equal moles contain equal numbers of molecules, and the subscripts in a formula count *moles of atoms* as well as atoms.

recap.nextHook: Moles let a reaction be read as a recipe, but only once its equation is written with every atom accounted for, and the next lesson shows how to balance one.

lessons.title: Keep every atom

steps.headline: An equation records atoms being rearranged, with none lost

lead.text: When hydrogen gas burns in chlorine, the molecules break apart and the atoms rejoin in new pairs, and the substance that results is hydrogen chloride. This is written as an equation, H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl, in which the substances on the left are the **reactants**, the substances on the right are the **products**, and the arrow reads "react to give". Each substance is written with its own formula, and the number in front says how many molecules take part.

The atoms are only rearranged. Antoine Lavoisier, whose careful weighings of substances before and after reactions in sealed vessels showed that the total mass does not change, set the principle out as an axiom in 1789, and the atomic account of it is that every atom on the left of an equation is an atom on the right. Each element must therefore appear **the same number of times on both sides**, and an equation that satisfies this is **balanced**.

steps.headline: Count each element on both sides, then adjust one coefficient and count again

lead.text: To balance an equation, write it with the correct formula for every substance, count each element on both sides, and wherever the counts differ change a [[coefficient|A number in front of a formula giving how many molecules or formula units there are. Met in “Reading a chemical formula”.]] and count again. Sodium burns in chlorine to make sodium chloride, Na + Cl₂ → NaCl, and counting gives 1 Na and 2 Cl on the left against 1 Na and 1 Cl on the right. The chlorine is *short* on the right, and a 2 in front of NaCl supplies it, giving 2 Na and 2 Cl there.

That change has upset the sodium, which is now 1 on the left and 2 on the right, so a 2 in front of Na restores it, and the equation 2 Na + Cl₂ → 2 NaCl has 2 Na and 2 Cl on each side. Changing one coefficient can disturb another element, so **recount every element after every change**.

steps.headline: Only coefficients may be changed, because a subscript names the substance

lead.text: In the sodium chloride equation there is a tempting shortcut: writing NaCl₂ in place of NaCl would put a second chlorine on the right in a single step. But NaCl₂ is not sodium chloride. Sodium forms Na⁺ and chlorine forms Cl⁻, which combine in the ratio 1 to 1, so a formula with two chlorine atoms for one sodium describes a substance that does not exist.

The [[subscripts|Small numbers after a symbol giving the atoms of that element in one unit of the substance. Met in “Reading a chemical formula”.]] of a formula belong to the substance, as the lesson on formulas showed, and **an equation can only change how much of each substance reacts, and never what the substances are**. A coefficient does exactly that, since it changes the number of units and leaves each unit as it was, which is why the coefficients are the only numbers to adjust when balancing.

steps.headline: Balancing K + Cl₂ → KCl

workedSteps.text: Counting gives 1 K and 2 Cl on the left, and 1 K and 1 Cl on the right, so chlorine is short by one on the right.
The fix has to leave the formula KCl alone, since K₂Cl would be a different substance, so a coefficient is used: 2 KCl supplies 2 Cl.
The right side now has 2 K, so 2 K on the left restores the balance, and a recount gives 2 K and 2 Cl on both sides.

steps.headline: Balancing CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O

workedSteps.text: Carbon is 1 on each side. Hydrogen is 4 on the left, so 2 H₂O gives 4 H on the right.
The right side now holds 2 + 2 = 4 oxygen atoms, and the O₂ on the left must supply all of them, at 2 atoms for each molecule.

steps.headline: Leave an element that stands alone until last

lead.text: A good order makes the work shorter. Begin with the elements that each appear in one substance on each side, and leave until last **any element that appears by itself**, such as the O₂ in a burning reaction, because changing the coefficient of a free element *does not* upset any other element. Burning propane, C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O, shows the order: 3 CO₂ balances the carbon and 4 H₂O balances the hydrogen, and only then are the oxygen atoms on the right counted, at 6 + 4 = 10, which 5 O₂ supplies.

If the oxygen atoms needed come to an odd number, one O₂ cannot supply them in whole molecules, and the remedy is to double every coefficient in the equation. The final check is the same each time: a recount of every element, with the left and right columns equal.

blocks.text: When carbon burns in too little air it forms carbon monoxide, and the reaction can be written C + O₂ → CO, which names what goes in and what comes out. Counted atom by atom, though, the line does not add up, because oxygen gas is made of two-atom molecules, so there are two oxygen atoms on the left and only one on the right. A chemical reaction only regroups atoms and never makes or destroys them, so a line that loses an atom cannot be a true account of what happens.

Putting such a line right is a matter of counting each element on both sides and choosing how many molecules of each substance take part, until every count agrees. An equation corrected in this way gives the exact proportions in which substances react, and those proportions are what you need in order to say how much of each substance a reaction uses and how much it makes.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to balance a chemical equation by choosing coefficients so that every element is counted equally on both sides.
intro.whyItMatters: A balanced equation is the recipe for a reaction, so the amounts in the next two lessons are read from it.

recap.keyIdea: A balanced equation has the same number of atoms of each element on both sides, reached by changing coefficients and never subscripts.

blocks.text: An equation lists the [[reactants|The substances that react, written on the left of the arrow. Met in “Keep every atom”.]] and the products, and it is **balanced** when each element is counted the same number of times on both sides. To balance it, count every element, change a coefficient where the counts differ, and recount, since one change can upset another element.
Only coefficients may be changed, because **a subscript names the substance**, and leaving an element that stands alone, such as O₂, until last usually makes the work shorter.

recap.nextHook: A balanced equation can also be read as a recipe in moles, which is how the next lesson finds how much of one substance reacts with or makes another.

lessons.title: Read a reaction as a ratio

steps.headline: Multiplying every coefficient by the same number gives the same reaction on a larger scale

lead.text: An equation such as H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl describes one molecule of each reactant, but it describes just as well three molecules of each, or a thousand, because every hydrogen molecule that reacts does so with one chlorine molecule and forms two of hydrogen chloride. Multiply every coefficient by the same number and the equation says the *same* thing at a larger scale, with the proportions unchanged: 3 H₂ + 3 Cl₂ → 6 HCl.

Multiply by 6.02214076 × 10²³, the number of particles in a [[mole|The amount of substance that contains 6.02214076 × 10²³ particles. Met in “From moles to mass”.]], and the coefficients become moles: 1 mol of H₂ and 1 mol of Cl₂ give 2 mol of HCl. The coefficients of a balanced equation are therefore **in the ratio of the moles of the substances**, and a quantity in moles is one that can be weighed out.

steps.headline: A mole ratio compares the moles of any two substances in the equation

lead.text: Any two coefficients of a [[balanced|An equation with the same number of atoms of each element on both sides. Met in “Keep every atom”.]] equation make a **mole ratio**. In N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃ the coefficients 1, 3 and 2 say that 1 mol of nitrogen reacts with 3 mol of hydrogen to form 2 mol of ammonia, so the mole ratio of hydrogen to ammonia is *3 to 2*, that of nitrogen to hydrogen is 1 to 3, and so on for each pair.

The process that Fritz Haber made work in the laboratory was taken to industrial scale by Carl Bosch's team at BASF, whose plant at Oppau began production in 1913. A plant of that kind depends on exactly these ratios, because they fix how much hydrogen must be supplied for a given amount of nitrogen.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows two balanced equations with their coefficients written out. Each pair of coefficients in either is a mole ratio.

steps.headline: A conversion factor scales a mole ratio to any amount

lead.text: To find the amount of one substance from the amount of another, multiply the amount you have by the mole ratio written as a fraction. For H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl, the ratio of HCl to H₂ is 2 mol to 1 mol, so 5 mol of H₂, with chlorine in excess, form 5 mol × (2 mol HCl ÷ 1 mol H₂) = 10 mol of HCl. A reactant is in *excess* when there is more of it than the reaction can use, so the hydrogen is used up first, and the amount of hydrogen is what sets the amount of product.

**Write the substance you have underneath** in the fraction, so that its moles cancel and the moles of the substance you want are left. The units then check the arrangement: if the moles of the given substance do not cancel, the fraction has been turned the wrong way up.

steps.headline: Finding the moles of Cl₂ for 10 mol of Na

workedSteps.text: The equation 2 Na + Cl₂ → 2 NaCl says that 2 mol of Na react with 1 mol of Cl₂, so the ratio is 1 mol of Cl₂ to 2 mol of Na.
To find the moles of Cl₂ for 10 mol of Na, multiply by the ratio written with Na underneath, so that the moles of Na cancel.
workedSteps.math: 10 mol Na × (1 mol Cl₂ ÷ 2 mol Na)

workedSteps.text: The moles of Na cancel, and 10 × 1/2 leaves 5 mol of Cl₂.

steps.headline: Finding the moles of H₂O from 3 mol of O₂

workedSteps.text: The equation 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O gives 2 mol of H₂O for every 1 mol of O₂, so the ratio of water to oxygen is 2 to 1.
Multiply the moles of O₂ by this ratio, with O₂ underneath so that its moles cancel.
workedSteps.math: 3 mol O₂ × (2 mol H₂O ÷ 1 mol O₂)

steps.headline: The ratio is a ratio of moles, and masses are not in the same proportions

lead.text: The coefficients count particles, so they are in the ratio of the *moles* and not of the masses. In N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, 1 mol of N₂ has a mass of 28 g, 3 mol of H₂ have a mass of 3 × 2 = 6 g, and 2 mol of NH₃ have a mass of 2 × 17 = 34 g. The masses add up across the arrow, as they must, since 28 + 6 = 34, but they are not in the ratio 1 : 3 : 2.

A problem that gives or asks for a mass therefore takes three steps: convert the mass to moles with the [[molar mass|The mass of one mole of a substance, in grams per mole. Met in “From moles to mass”.]], apply the mole ratio, and convert the result back to a mass if one is wanted. The mole ratio is applied to **moles and never directly to grams**.

steps.headline: The same method works from a product back to a reactant

lead.text: Nothing in the method depends on which substance is a reactant and which a product. The amount you have may be a product, and the amount you want a reactant. In H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl, 8 mol of HCl need 8 mol × (1 mol Cl₂ ÷ 2 mol HCl) = 4 mol of Cl₂, since 1 mol of chlorine is used for every 2 mol of hydrogen chloride formed.

In every case **the moles wanted equal the moles given times the coefficient of the substance wanted divided by the coefficient of the substance given**. A quick check on size helps: a substance with a *larger* coefficient than the one you started from always has a larger amount, and one with a *smaller* coefficient always has a smaller amount.

blocks.text: The equation N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃ is the recipe for ammonia, which Fritz Haber first made from its elements in the laboratory in 1909. Read as a sentence it says that one molecule of nitrogen reacts with three of hydrogen to form two of ammonia, which is true but of little direct use at the bench, since molecules cannot be counted out one at a time.

What a chemist needs to know is how much hydrogen a given amount of nitrogen needs, and how much ammonia will result. The coefficients answer both questions once they are read as amounts in moles, because a mole is a fixed number of molecules that can be weighed out, so the proportions that hold for single molecules hold for moles as well.

intro.whyItMatters: Predicting how much product a reaction can make, or how much reactant it needs, starts with exactly this ratio.

recap.keyIdea: The coefficients of a balanced equation are the ratio of the moles of its substances, so the moles of any substance follow from the moles of another.

blocks.text: The coefficients of a balanced equation are a ratio of **moles**, so the equation can be scaled to any amount: moles wanted = moles given × (coefficient wanted ÷ coefficient given). Writing the given substance underneath makes its moles cancel and leaves the moles of the substance wanted.

The ratio holds for moles, not for masses, so a mass has to be turned into moles with the [[molar mass|The mass of one mole of a substance, in grams per mole. Met in “From moles to mass”.]] first and turned back at the end, and the same method works from a product to a reactant as well as from a reactant to a product.

lessons.title: The reactant that runs out

steps.headline: A reaction runs in batches, and its supplies decide how many

lead.text: In 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O one **batch** of the reaction uses 2 mol of hydrogen and 1 mol of oxygen and forms 2 mol of water. A reaction can run through as many batches as its supplies allow, using the same amounts in each, so with 4 mol of hydrogen and 2 mol of oxygen it runs two batches and forms 4 mol of water.

Supplies are *not* usually in the ratio of the equation. Each reactant can support only so many batches, found by dividing its amount by its coefficient: 8 mol of hydrogen can support 8 ÷ 2 = 4 batches, and 3 mol of oxygen can support 3 ÷ 1 = 3. The reaction can run only **as many batches as the scarcer reactant allows**, which here is 3, so the oxygen is used up first, 6 mol of water forms, and 8 − 3 × 2 = 2 mol of hydrogen remain.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows that case and a second, with the supplies drawn as columns. The progress slider runs the batches, and the reactant that reaches zero first is the one that stops the reaction.

steps.headline: The reactant that supports fewer batches runs out first and sets the yield

lead.text: The reactant that supports the fewest batches is used up first, and it is the **limiting reactant**. Every other reactant is then in **excess**, which means that some of it will be left over, and the amount of product that can form is fixed by the limiting reactant alone. The *most* product that the supplies allow is the **theoretical yield**, and it is the number of batches times the amount of product that one batch forms.

The method has three steps. Divide the amount of each reactant by its coefficient to find the batches it supports, take the smaller number as the number of batches the reaction can run, and multiply by the coefficient of the product. In H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl, 5 mol of H₂ and 3 mol of Cl₂ support 5 and 3 batches, so chlorine limits the reaction to 3 batches, and the yield is 3 × 2 = 6 mol of HCl.

steps.headline: Finding the yield from 5 mol of N₂ and 6 mol of H₂

workedSteps.text: One batch of N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃ uses 1 mol of N₂ and 3 mol of H₂, so 5 mol of N₂ support 5 batches and 6 mol of H₂ support 2.
The reaction can run only 2 batches, because by then the hydrogen is used up, so hydrogen is the limiting reactant.
Each batch forms 2 mol of NH₃, so the theoretical yield is 2 batches times 2 mol.

steps.headline: Finding the yield from 4 mol of N₂ and 3 mol of H₂

workedSteps.text: In N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, 4 mol of N₂ support 4 batches and 3 mol of H₂ support 3 ÷ 3 = 1 batch, so hydrogen limits the reaction to one batch.
Each batch forms 2 mol of NH₃, so the yield is the number of batches times the amount one batch forms.

steps.headline: The leftover is what the limiting reactant did not use up

lead.text: The limiting reactant is used up completely, and the excess reactant leaves a remainder that is found in two steps: the amount used is the number of batches times its coefficient, and **the amount left is the amount supplied minus the amount used**. The number of batches need not be a *whole number*. With 5 mol of magnesium and 4 mol of oxygen in 2 Mg + O₂ → 2 MgO, the magnesium supports 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5 batches and the oxygen 4, so the reaction runs 2.5 batches, forms 2.5 × 2 = 5 mol of MgO and uses 2.5 mol of oxygen, which leaves 4 − 2.5 = 1.5 mol.

If the supplies are in exactly the [[mole ratio|A comparison of the moles of two substances, taken from the coefficients of a balanced equation. Met in “Read a reaction as a ratio”.]] of the equation, every reactant supports the same number of batches, all of them are used up together, and nothing is left over.

afterFigure.text: The first case in the figure is the example above. In the second, 6 mol of magnesium and 3 mol of oxygen support the same number of batches, and the leftovers are both zero.

steps.headline: Check the answer by accounting for every atom

lead.text: A result can be checked by counting atoms, as for a [[balanced|An equation with the same number of atoms of each element on both sides. Met in “Keep every atom”.]] equation. For 5 mol of H₂ and 3 mol of Cl₂, the earlier result was 6 mol of HCl with 2 mol of H₂ left over. Before the reaction there are 5 × 2 = 10 mol of H atoms and 3 × 2 = 6 mol of Cl atoms. Afterwards, 6 mol of HCl hold 6 mol of H and 6 mol of Cl, and the 2 mol of H₂ hold 4 mol of H, so there are 10 mol of H and 6 mol of Cl again.

The theoretical yield is an upper limit. It is what the reaction would form if every batch ran to completion, and real reactions often give *less*, because some of the reactants are lost to other reactions or stay behind with the product. The limiting reactant **sets what is possible**, and the theoretical yield is the most that the supplies allow.

lessons.orientation: How to find the limiting reactant, the theoretical yield and the leftover from the amounts supplied.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: In 1805 Alexander von Humboldt and Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac burned mixtures of hydrogen and oxygen and found that the two gases combine to form water in a fixed proportion, very nearly two volumes of hydrogen to one of oxygen. Whatever was supplied in addition to that proportion was not used, and it remained as gas when the reaction was over.

Reactants are rarely supplied in exactly the ratio of the equation, so one of them is used up first and the other is left, and it is the one used up that decides how much product can form. Finding it, and counting what it leaves behind, takes only the mole ratios from the previous lesson.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the reactant that runs out, the most product a reaction can make, and the amount left over.
intro.whyItMatters: Real reactions are never supplied in perfect ratios, so this is how chemists predict what comes out and what is wasted.

recap.keyIdea: The reactant that supports the fewest batches limits the reaction, and it sets the theoretical yield, while the other reactants leave a remainder.

blocks.text: A reaction runs in **batches** of the amounts in the equation. Dividing each reactant's amount by its coefficient gives the batches it supports, and **the smallest number identifies the limiting reactant**, which sets the theoretical yield: batches times the coefficient of the product.

Every other reactant is in excess, and what remains is the amount supplied minus the amount used, while supplies in exactly the ratio of the equation leave nothing. This is the end of the chain that the course built: counts of particles give formulas, formulas give masses, masses give moles, and moles with a balanced equation give the amounts of everything a reaction uses and makes.

questions.prompt: Oxygen has 8 protons, 8 neutrons and 8 electrons. What is its atomic number?
hints: Choose the particle that identifies the element.
Z counts protons; it ignores neutrons and electrons.
Which supplied count is the definition of atomic number?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Atomic number counts protons, so Z = 8.

questions.onCorrect: 8. The atomic number is the proton count, whatever the neutrons and electrons are doing.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the neutrons. The atomic number counts one kind of particle only.

questions.prompt: One carbon atom has 6 neutrons and another has 7. Why are both of them carbon?
hints: Which particle count names an element?
Compare the proton counts of the two atoms.

acceptedIdeas: Their proton counts agree
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each nucleus still contains six protons.

questions.onCorrect: Both nuclei contain 6 protons, and the proton count alone fixes the element, so the extra neutron makes the second atom heavier without making it anything other than carbon.
